title: A Power Cut at Every Step: Two Slots and a Commit, and Why Overwriting the Running Release Bricks the Robot

questions.question: Why does copying the new release over the running one brick the robot when the power fails?
options: For the time it takes the slot is half old and half new, with the old hash, and there is no other slot to boot

questions.question: In the two slot install, what is the last step and why last?
options: The move of the boot pointer: nothing before it changes what boots, and it is one write
questions.explanation: After nine of ten steps the robot still boots release 1.

questions.question: After the ninth of ten steps, which release does the robot boot?
options: Release 1: release 2 is complete and valid in the other slot but the pointer has not moved
questions.explanation: The old release is untouched until the last step.

questions.question: Why can a cut install simply be run again?
options: The plan is made from what boots now and not from where the last attempt stopped, so it needs no memory of the failure

questions.question: A chunk of the new release is damaged after the switch. What boots?
options: The release before, from the other slot: the slot is invalid and the fallback is the design

questions.question: What does this scheme assume about the hardware that you must test on the real robot?
options: That a single write is atomic, so that a power cut falls between steps and never inside one: pull the real power hundreds of times
questions.explanation: Flash that tears a write breaks the whole argument.
